documents: A new hand-held tool can reliably measure tiny, involuntary eye movements in people with Parkinson's Disease, and these movements are generally slower in people with the condition compared to healthy adults of similar age.
The evidence shows the tool gives consistent results when used repeatedly, but it does not show that taking medication for Parkinson's Disease changes the speed of these eye movements.
A quick and comfortable eye test could help doctors find or track certain health conditions earlier, but more research is needed to be sure it works well.

Current ways to measure tiny, constant eye movements are uncomfortable and require putting a probe directly on the eye, which can cause dryness and require the patient to hold their eye open for a long time.
Scientists do not yet fully understand what causes these tiny eye movements, though they are thought to be linked to activity in the lower part of the brain.

A new handheld device can measure a tiny, involuntary eye movement in people with Parkinson's disease using safe laser technology in just three seconds. This quick and comfortable test provides a reliable way to distinguish people with the condition from healthy older adults, potentially helping with earlier diagnosis.

The eye movement measured by the device is linked to specific symptoms like facial expression difficulties and walking problems, but it does not change when people take standard Parkinson's disease medication. This suggests the measurement reflects brain chemistry beyond the main chemical system targeted by current treatments.

While this new test shows promise for complementing existing tools for earlier diagnosis or disease monitoring, larger studies are needed to confirm these findings before it can be widely used in clinical practice.
The research team planned to test if a wearable device could reliably measure hand tremors in people with Parkinson's disease and check if the readings matched the severity of their condition.

The study only included people with confirmed Parkinson's disease and healthy older adults, while excluding anyone with mental health problems, head injuries, eye conditions, or significant memory issues.

The specific brain regions and chemical systems responsible for the involuntary trembling of eye muscles in Parkinson's disease are not yet fully understood, though the condition is known to damage these areas early in the disease course. This lack of understanding means it is currently unclear exactly which parts of the brain are failing to control eye movements in affected people.

A new, small, and portable device that uses laser technology to measure eye muscle tremors has been developed, but it has not yet been proven to be accurate or reliable for people with Parkinson's disease. Until this new tool is validated, it cannot be used to help diagnose or monitor the condition in a clinical setting.

This initial study aimed to check if the new portable eye-tremor measuring device is consistent when used repeatedly on people with Parkinson's disease and if it is practical to use in real-world clinical settings. The researchers expected that this new tool would be both reliable and feasible for use with patients who have Parkinson's disease.

People with Parkinson's disease in the study had mild to moderate symptoms and their overall thinking ability remained strong. Their thinking ability stayed strong whether they were taking their medication or not.

The device used to measure tremor gave very consistent results when tested twice on the same person. There were no safety problems or device failures during the study, and a reading could always be obtained even if a participant blinked or moved their eyes.

The study involved people with Parkinson's disease and healthy individuals, with some participants tested at home and others in a laboratory setting. The research team used a single device and the same operator for all measurements to ensure consistency.

Researchers collected information about participants' age, gender, education, fear of falling, vision, and specific details about their Parkinson's disease, such as how long they had the condition and how severe it was.
Measurements were taken while participants sat in a chair looking straight ahead in a quiet, well-lit room. The team averaged three readings for each eye to get a reliable result.
To see how medication affects eye movements, participants were tested before taking their morning dose of Parkinson's medication and then tested again one hour after taking it.
The data was analyzed using standard statistical software, and any readings that could not be obtained were treated as missing and excluded from the final results.
Because this was an early-stage investigation, the researchers did not adjust for multiple comparisons, which might make the results less conservative than in larger studies.
The researchers checked if the eye movement measurement could tell the difference between people with Parkinson's disease and healthy people by comparing the two groups.
The new eye movement measurement tool provided consistent and reliable results, suggesting it is accurate enough to be trusted for future use in tracking health conditions.

The study found that taking the specific medication for Parkinson's disease did not change the eye movement measurements, meaning this tool does not currently show how well the medication is working for an individual.

A test measuring tiny, involuntary eye movements can help identify people with Parkinson's disease, but it is not a perfect tool and may fail to detect the condition in some cases or incorrectly flag healthy people.
The research did not show that the speed of these tiny eye movements is linked to how severe a person's Parkinson's disease symptoms are or how long they have had the condition.

People living with Parkinson's disease blink at a noticeably slower rate than healthy people, and this difference is large enough to be clearly seen in measurements. The evidence strongly supports that this slower blinking is a real feature of the condition.

The measurement of blink rate can help identify people with Parkinson's disease, but it is not perfect and cannot be used as the only tool for diagnosis. This test does not show how well the blink rate changes when a person takes their medication.

In people with Parkinson's disease, a slower blink rate is linked to having more trouble with speech and facial movements. This connection suggests that the blink measurement reflects the severity of these specific physical symptoms.

The specific brain pathways and chemical systems responsible for the measured eye muscle activity in people with Parkinson's disease remain unknown, so more research is needed to understand how this measurement works and how it can be used in healthcare.

Standard Parkinson's medications did not change the measured eye muscle activity in people with Parkinson's disease, suggesting that other brain chemicals besides dopamine are likely involved in this specific eye movement.

The evidence indicates that the measured eye muscle activity is not controlled by the dopamine system, but the exact brain mechanisms are still uncertain and require further study to be useful in clinical trials.
The eye movement measurement tool did not cause any harm or make people want to stop the study, and minor issues like blinking did not prevent the researchers from getting the necessary readings.
The eye movement test can help doctors tell apart people with Parkinson's disease from healthy people, but it is not perfect on its own because the results sometimes overlap between the two groups.

Because the test results can overlap, this measurement is better used as one part of a larger set of tests to help doctors make decisions, especially when symptoms are unclear, rather than as the only way to diagnose the condition.
Older people tend to have slower eye movements than younger people, which is likely due to natural changes in the brain and nerves that control how eyes move as a person ages.

The study found that people who accumulated sleep debt performed slower on a specific attention test, but this does not prove they are as dangerous as intoxicated drivers because the lab test does not measure real-world driving behavior. The evidence shows a strong link between sleep loss and slower processing, but it does not confirm that this specific type of impairment causes actual car accidents.

A study found that people with Parkinson's disease who used a special treadmill that supports their body weight walked faster, took longer steps, and had better balance than people who received standard physical therapy. This type of training also reduced the fear of falling and improved the overall quality of life for the participants.

Freezing of gait is a disabling movement problem that affects nearly half of people with Parkinson's disease, increasing the risk of falls and reducing independence. Even after medication or other medical treatments, these movement problems often remain, showing the need for additional rehabilitation strategies.

The study involved forty people with Parkinson's disease who had difficulty walking, and the researchers only had preliminary data to guide future larger studies rather than definitive proof of the treatment's effect.

The study included people between fifty and eighty-five years old who had a confirmed diagnosis of Parkinson's disease and difficulty walking, but excluded those with heart, lung, or bone problems that would make exercise unsafe.

The study compared two groups of twenty people each, where one group received a special treadmill exercise program alongside standard care while the other group only did traditional physical exercise, and the people measuring the results did not know which group each person was in.

A small early study suggests that walking on a treadmill that partially supports the body's weight might help people with Parkinson's disease walk better, stand more steadily, and feel better about their daily lives. The researchers are not certain this works because the study was small and need a larger group of people to confirm these results.

Parkinson's disease is a condition that causes problems with movement, balance, and thinking, and it is the second most common type of brain disease that gets worse over time. One serious symptom is freezing of gait, where a person suddenly cannot start or keep walking, which makes falling more likely and makes it harder to live independently.

Because many people with Parkinson's disease do not get enough help from pills or surgery for freezing of gait, doctors are looking for other treatments like physical therapy that do not involve drugs or surgery. Using a machine that reduces the weight on the legs during walking may let patients practice walking safely with less strain on their joints and a lower risk of falling.
Because the study involved a small number of people and measured many different outcomes, the results should be viewed with caution and are not definitive proof of an effect.
The researchers did not directly compare the amount of change between the start and end of the study because this method is known to create misleading errors in small groups.
The study measured how patients walk and how steady they are to see if therapy helps them move better and track their progress over time.
The study also looked at how worried people are about falling, their overall quality of life, and how severe their anxiety symptoms are.
The walking tests were done at the start of the study and again after treatment to check for changes in how the patients move.
The study measured how well people could balance, move, and walk to see if their risk of falling was high or low.
The study also looked at how people felt about their daily lives, their worry about falling, and their levels of anxiety.
One test involved standing still with eyes open and closed to check if a person's body weight was evenly distributed and stable.
The study involved a small group of people, so the results should be viewed with caution and are not definitive proof of the treatment's effect.
People in the treatment group showed better quality of life, mobility, and balance compared to the control group after the intervention.
The two groups were similar in age, gender, and education at the start of the study, but the treatment group had more severe movement and thinking problems initially.
People who received the gait training intervention likely experienced real improvements in how they walk and balance because the group that did not receive the treatment did not show similar changes.

The study found that people who reported better mobility and emotional well-being also tended to have specific physical walking patterns, such as longer steps or smoother movement, but this does not prove that one causes the other.

The gait training program helped people walk faster, take longer steps, and improve their balance and stability, which suggests the treatment is useful for maintaining physical function and emotional health.

People who received the intervention reported feeling healthier and more independent in their daily lives. The evidence strongly suggests that this improvement in their perceived health status was caused by the treatment itself, as people in the comparison group did not experience similar changes.

Participants in the experimental group walked faster and moved with greater ease after the intervention. The evidence strongly supports that these gains in mobility and walking speed were due to the specific treatment received, rather than natural changes over time.

The intervention led to better balance and steadier posture for the participants. The evidence is very strong that these improvements in physical stability were a direct result of the treatment, as the control group showed no such progress.

People in the experimental group demonstrated better endurance and the ability to walk longer distances. The evidence strongly indicates that this increased capacity for physical activity was caused by the intervention, not by other factors.

Participants showed more efficient and controlled walking patterns after the intervention. The evidence strongly suggests that these improvements in how they moved were due to the treatment, as the control group did not show similar changes in their gait.

The study found that a specific type of treadmill exercise helped people with Parkinson's disease balance better and walk with longer steps, which may lower their risk of falling. However, the evidence is not strong enough to be certain because the group of people tested was small, so larger studies are needed to confirm these benefits.

A small early study suggests that walking on a treadmill with special air pressure support might help people with Parkinson's disease walk faster, take longer steps, and feel more stable. However, because the study was small and short-term, it is not yet certain if this treatment works long-term or is better than other therapies.

An initial small-scale test found that a specific treadmill exercise helped people with Parkinson's disease walk better and feel less afraid of falling. These results are promising but need to be checked in larger studies to confirm if the benefits last over time.

People living with schizophrenia may have a higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease, though the evidence is not definitive because previous research did not consider the effects of the medications used to treat schizophrenia.
Schizophrenia involves symptoms like seeing or hearing things that are not there and feeling emotionally flat or lacking motivation, and its exact cause is still unknown.
The study aims to find out if people with schizophrenia have a higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease and whether the medications used to treat schizophrenia affect that risk.
Researchers compared patients with schizophrenia to other people to see if the condition itself or the drugs taken for it lead to a greater likelihood of developing Parkinson's disease.

People with schizophrenia face a much higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease compared to people without the condition. The evidence for this increased risk is described as significant, but it does not prove that schizophrenia directly causes the movement disorder.

Using the medication risperidone for schizophrenia is linked to a higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease, while using quetiapine is linked to a lower chance. This finding highlights the need for doctors to closely watch patients with schizophrenia for signs of movement problems, though more research is needed to fully understand these long-term medication effects.

Parkinson's disease is the second most common degenerative brain disorder and is more common in men than women. The condition involves symptoms like slow movement, stiffness, and shaking, and its exact causes are still not fully understood.
The study compared people with schizophrenia to a separate group of people without the condition, matching them by age, gender, and general health status.
The study looked at whether people with schizophrenia are more likely to develop Parkinson's disease, and it also checked if the specific mood-altering medications they take are linked to that risk.
To make sure the diagnosis of Parkinson's disease was accurate, the researchers required a hospital admission or two separate doctor visits confirming the condition within a one-year period.
The analysis adjusted for many other health conditions and mental health issues to ensure the results were not simply due to these other factors.

The study looked at people with schizophrenia and people without the condition to see if the mental health condition is linked to developing Parkinson's disease. The researchers also checked if the specific medications taken for schizophrenia at the start of the diagnosis affect the risk of developing Parkinson's disease.

The research used health records from a national insurance system in South Korea to track people from 2010 to 2021. Parkinson's disease is a recognized serious illness in this system that requires a doctor to confirm the diagnosis using standard guidelines.

The study focused on adults who were newly diagnosed with schizophrenia during the observation period, excluding those who already had the condition at the start. The data could not be shared publicly because of privacy laws that protect individual health records.

People living with schizophrenia have a significantly higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease compared to people without the condition. The evidence for this link is very strong, with a narrow range of uncertainty that confirms the increased risk is real.
Men have a slightly higher risk of developing Parkinson's disease than women. This finding is supported by confident evidence, though the difference in risk between the sexes is modest.

Certain other health conditions, such as specific stress-related disorders, stroke, head injuries, and osteoarthritis, are also linked to a higher risk of developing Parkinson's disease. The study confirms these associations exist but does not show that they are the only factors involved.

People with schizophrenia are more likely to have other health problems and use more medications than people without the condition. This finding is based on a clear comparison between the two groups, but it does not prove that these extra conditions or medications cause the higher risk of Parkinson's disease.

People living with schizophrenia have a significantly higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease over a ten-year period compared to people without the condition. The evidence for this long-term risk is very strong and consistent across different time periods.

Using antipsychotic medications is linked to a slightly higher likelihood of developing Parkinson's disease in people with schizophrenia. However, this finding does not prove that the medications cause the condition, only that the two are associated.

Among other health conditions, anxiety and stress-related disorders are the most strongly linked to the development of Parkinson's disease in people with schizophrenia. This association is stronger than the link seen with other common health issues like heart disease or diabetes.

People with schizophrenia have a much higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease compared to people without schizophrenia, and this link remains strong even after accounting for other health factors. The evidence is very confident in this connection, but the study does not prove that schizophrenia causes Parkinson's disease.

People who take quetiapine for mental health conditions have a lower chance of developing Parkinson's disease, while people who take risperidone have a higher chance compared to people who do not take these medications. The study shows a clear difference in risk for these specific groups, but it does not show that the medications directly cause or prevent the disease.
People who take antipsychotic medications have a slightly higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease compared to people who do not take these medications.

The study found that people taking the specific medication risperidone have a higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease, while people taking the specific medication quetiapine have a slightly lower chance.

People with schizophrenia who take a specific type of antipsychotic medication called risperidone have a higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease compared to people with schizophrenia who do not take that medication. The evidence strongly supports this increased risk, but it does not prove that the medication causes the disease.

People with schizophrenia who take antipsychotic medications generally have a significantly higher risk of developing Parkinson's disease than people with schizophrenia who do not take these medications. This finding is based on strong statistical evidence, but it does not show that the medication directly causes the condition.

Having schizophrenia itself is strongly associated with a much higher risk of developing Parkinson's disease compared to people without the condition. This link is very clear in the data, but it does not explain why the risk is higher or whether other factors are involved.

Men with schizophrenia have a slightly higher risk of developing Parkinson's disease than women with schizophrenia. This difference is small but consistent across the analysis, though it does not indicate a cause-and-effect relationship.

People with schizophrenia who also have certain mental health conditions, such as anxiety or stress-related disorders, have a higher risk of developing Parkinson's disease. The evidence for this link is strong, but it does not show that these mental health conditions cause Parkinson's disease.

People with schizophrenia who have a history of head injury have a higher risk of developing Parkinson's disease than those without such a history. The connection is well-supported by the data, but it does not prove that the injury causes the disease.

People with schizophrenia who have cerebrovascular disease, such as strokes, have a higher risk of developing Parkinson's disease. The evidence for this association is strong, but it does not show that the cerebrovascular disease causes Parkinson's disease.

People who take the antipsychotic medication quetiapine have a lower chance of developing Parkinson's disease compared to people who do not take any antipsychotic medication. People who take the antipsychotic medication risperidone have a higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease compared to people who do not take any antipsychotic medication.

The strong link between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease may be explained by shared biological mechanisms, particularly the imbalance of dopamine in the brain. These opposing pathways in the brain may make people with schizophrenia more vulnerable to developing Parkinson's disease.

A head injury may increase the risk of developing Parkinson's disease through damage to nerve fibers and impaired transport in the brain. This injury influences the formation of specific pathological proteins that are closely linked to Parkinson's disease.

People with schizophrenia who also have blood vessel problems in the brain, such as a previous stroke, face a higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease because these conditions can worsen the damage to nerve cells.

Individuals with schizophrenia who suffer from anxiety or stress-related disorders are more likely to develop Parkinson's disease, as these mental health conditions may speed up the process of nerve cell death.

Taking antipsychotic medications for schizophrenia is linked to a slightly higher risk of developing Parkinson's disease, although the specific effect varies depending on which medication is used and how long it is taken.

Symptoms of movement problems caused by antipsychotic drugs usually improve after stopping the medication, but some people may still develop the permanent degenerative form of Parkinson's disease even after the drug is withdrawn.
The study found a link between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease, but the evidence only shows an association and does not prove that one condition causes the other.
The findings may not apply to everyone because the study relied on hospital records rather than detailed medical tests or information about how severe the illness was.

The research could not determine the exact amounts of medication taken or how long people took them, which limits the ability to explain how specific drugs might affect the risk of developing Parkinson's disease.

Researchers caution that the study results should be interpreted with care because the link between the mental health condition and the movement disorder might be partly due to the medications used to treat the mental health condition rather than the condition itself.

The study found a connection between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease in a large group of people in Korea, but it does not explain the biological reasons behind this link or how different amounts of medication affect the risk.

Because the study did not correct for the chance of finding false patterns in the data, the claim that specific brain wave frequencies are a reliable sign of Parkinson's disease is likely overstated. This means the current findings should be viewed as a preliminary hint rather than a proven diagnostic tool for patients.

The study does not prove that the anti-gravity system restores natural walking mechanics, as it only shows improvement while the body is partially supported, leaving open the possibility that the observed gains are entirely due to the specific expertise of the shared physiotherapists rather than the technology.

The finding that unloading treadmill training improves walking speed is consistent with previous research, but the small number of participants means we cannot be confident that the improvement was not due to chance. Therefore, while the method shows promise, the evidence is not strong enough to guarantee it works for everyone.

We cannot trust the claim that the measurement tool is consistent because the researchers did not record details like sleep, caffeine, or medication timing, which means the results might reflect temporary lifestyle factors rather than a stable biological trait.

The findings from the different studies cannot be combined to answer whether these tools actually help patients manage their disease because they were not designed to work together, leaving the overall impact on patient outcomes unknown.

While digital tools show promise for detecting movement disorders early, they currently function as separate, unconnected measurements rather than a single, reliable diagnostic system. This lack of a unified approach means doctors cannot yet use these tools to make standardized decisions about changing a patient's medication or care plan.

The microtremor protocol cannot reliably trigger a clinical decision because it lacks documentation of the precise environmental controls, such as lighting conditions and camera distance. Without these details, we cannot confirm that the measurement process is stable enough to be trusted for making medical judgments, as the signal filtering is sensitive to variations in ambient light.

Patients should expect that their monitoring involves specific, controlled setups like fixed camera distances and controlled lighting, because the data is only interpretable under these strict conditions. The initial readings are not definitive without these environmental controls, and it is unclear how these specific settings will be standardized across different clinics.

documents: The study included 33 participants with Parkinson's Disease and 31 age-matched healthy controls.

For analytical validation, 22 participants with Parkinson's Disease completed a test-retest reliability assessment of Ocular Microtremor measurement, which was assessed using interclass correlation coefficients (ICC).
The Ocular Microtremor measurement was acquired using the hand-held device known as the iTremor ONE.

For clinical validation, the Ocular Microtremor frequency in the 33 participants with Parkinson's Disease was compared to the 31 healthy controls, and correlations were explored with demographics and clinical scales.

Twenty-four participants with Parkinson's Disease were tested in both 'OFF' (12-hour withdrawal) and 'ON' anti-Parkinson's dopaminergic medication states to compare Ocular Microtremor response to the medication intervention.
The study used the iTremor ONE device, provided by Head Diagnostics, to measure ocular microtremor (OMT) non-invasively in just three seconds using safe laser technology.

The study used the iTremor ONE device from Head Diagnostics Ltd., Dublin, Ireland, which employs laser technology to measure Ocular Motor Tremor (OMT) with high resolution in a non-invasive, compact, and portable format.
The pilot study design aimed to examine the analytical and clinical validation of OMT measurement via the iTremor ONE in a Parkinson's Disease (PD) population.

The analytical validation component of the study specifically investigated the test-retest reliability of the iTremor ONE in measuring OMT frequency in Hertz (Hz) in people with Parkinson's Disease (PwPD).
The study also investigated the feasibility of measuring Ocular Motor Tremor (OMT) using hand-held technology in a real-world clinical setting with people with Parkinson's Disease (PwPD).

Existing methods for measuring ocular microtremor (OMT) rely on invasive tools such as the piezoelectric strain gauge technique, accelerometer fixed contact lenses, or eyelid fixed accelerometers, which require the eyes to be anaesthetised and cause discomfort and eye dryness.

The piezoelectric strain gauge technique requires constant uninterrupted contact with the sclera, meaning patients had their eye held open for up to 60 minutes at a time, and there is an unknown loading effect of the probe.
Video based eye-tracking systems do not possess the sensitivity required to detect ocular microtremor (OMT), which limits the generalisability and interpretation of underlying deficits.
Existing OMT measurement techniques possess high interobserver variability and require a highly trained operator.

The study was registered with Clinicaltrials.gov (NCT06051877) and received approval from the Northumbria University research ethics committee (Project No. 0034), the NHS Research Ethics Committee (REF: 23/WM/0004), and the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (REF: CI/2023/0031/GB).

Parkinson's disease participants were recruited from the Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust movement disorders clinic and local Parkinson's disease support groups, while age-matched healthy controls were recruited from family members of Parkinson's disease patients and Northumbria University staff, requiring a minimum age of 50 years for healthy controls.

Parkinson's disease participants were included based on a diagnosis according to UK brain bank criteria, and all participants were excluded if they had psychiatric co-morbidity, head injury, ocular disease such as cataracts, or severe cognitive impairment defined by a Montreal Cognitive Assessment score of less than 21.
Ocular motor tremor (OMT) was measured using the iTremor ONE device (Head Diagnostics Ltd., Dublin, Ireland) with software version 0.19, which records a three-second signal per eye after alignment.
The iTremor ONE device measures OMT by determining angular displacement from laser speckle correlation of images recorded in the Fourier plane of a lens.
The iTremor ONE device segregates OMT from other eye movements, hand movements, and subtle head movements using filtering techniques, including band-pass filtering.

Twenty-two participants with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) underwent two home-based assessments exactly one week apart, conducted at the same time of day (within 30 minutes) and in the same location in the home.

Disease severity was assessed in the "ON" state, one hour following Levodopa medication intake, using the Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson's disease Rating scale part III (UPDRS-III) during both visits.
For OMT measurement, participants sat in a high-backed chair with room lighting dimmed by closing curtains or blinds, and removed any glasses or contact lenses before the recording.
The OMT measurement involved directing a low-level laser onto the sclera for approximately three seconds while participants maintained a relaxed gaze at a target positioned on the wall at eye level.
If a participant blinked during the OMT recording, the reading was repeated, and three readings taken for each eye were averaged to provide a frequency reading in Hz.
A single iTremor ONE device was used for all measurements in the study, and the same operator performed every measurement.
The study used a single iTremor ONE device for all measurements, with the same operator conducting every assessment to ensure consistency.

Clinical validation included 33 people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD), of which 22 were assessed in the home environment and 11 in the laboratory, along with 31 healthy controls (HCs) assessed in the laboratory.
For the medication response assessment, 24 PwPD participants were required to abstain from dopaminergic medication for a minimum of 12 hours prior to the testing visit to establish the 'OFF' state.
Participants in the medication response assessment took their morning dose of levodopa and waited 60 minutes before their OMT frequency was assessed again in the 'ON' state.

OMT readings were taken with participants seated in a high-backed chair looking straight ahead at a target at eye level, in a quiet environment with controlled room lighting, and three measures per eye were averaged.
Data was analyzed using SPSS version 28 (IBM Inc, IL, USA), with normal distribution confirmed using Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Shapiro-Wilk tests (all Shapiro-Wilk p>.05).
The study did not control for multiple comparison corrections (e.g., Bonferroni) due to its exploratory nature, which may bias the results by increasing the risk of false positives.
Reliability was assessed using intra-class correlations (ICC2,1) and Pearson's correlations with Bland-Altman graphs to compare OMT between two sessions.

Known groups validity was examined using an ANOVA with group (PwPD vs. HCs) as a between-subject factor, followed by Tukey post-hoc analysis and Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis to calculate AUC, sensitivity, and specificity.
The optimal cut-off point for each outcome measure was determined as the point closest to corner (0,1) with a false positive rate of 0% and 100% sensitivity in the ROC plane.

Convergent validity was assessed by correlating OMT frequencies with demographic and clinical measures, using Pearson's correlation for normally distributed data and Spearman's correlation for non-normally distributed data.
Paired t-tests were performed with medication-state groups ('ON' vs 'OFF' medication) to examine whether OMT reduces in the 'OFF' medication state in Parkinson's disease.

The analytical validation cohort consisted of 22 people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) who had mild to moderate disease severity and preserved global cognition with a Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score of approximately 27.

The clinical validation cohort consisted of 33 people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) and 31 healthy controls (HC) who were age-matched, with PwPD having mild to moderate disease severity and a Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score of approximately 27.

The response to known intervention cohort consisted of 24 people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) who had mild to moderate disease severity and preserved global cognition with Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores of approximately 27 when 'OFF' medication and approximately 26 when 'ON' medication.
Test-retest reliability of OMT frequency measurements at home visits demonstrated excellent agreement with all Intraclass Correlation Coefficients (ICC) greater than 0.90.

The mean difference between OMT readings from the first and second visits was 1.14 Hz in the right eye (Limits of agreement 6.6%), 1.70 Hz in the left eye (Limits of agreement 7.4%), and 1.73 Hz in both eyes (Limits of agreement 7.5%).

OMT measurements were occasionally repeated by the examiner if the iTremor ONE device reported an inability to take a reading, typically due to eye blinks, obstruction from eye lashes or lids, or changes in gaze direction, but the required number of recordings was always obtained within a timely manner.
The study used the iTremor ONE technology, which employs a novel laser-speckle technique, to measure ocular microtremor (OMT) frequency in Hz.
The analytical validation of the iTremor ONE OMT measurement demonstrated excellent agreement with an Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) greater than 0.9 for OMT frequency detection.
The study design included a comparison of OMT frequency readings when participants were 'OFF' versus 'ON' anti-Parkinson's medication to assess the response to a known intervention.

The study compared Ocular Microtremor (OMT) frequency between People with Parkinson's Disease (PwPD) and Healthy Controls (HC), utilizing the MDS Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale III (UPDRS) and Hohen & Yahr Stage (H&Y) for clinical assessment.

The study evaluated the diagnostic utility of OMT frequency using Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves, reporting Area Under the Curve (AUC) values of 0.745 for the right eye, 0.773 for the left eye, and 0.760 for both eyes combined to differentiate PwPD from HCs.

The study analyzed the relationship between average OMT frequency and clinical measures including Age, Sex, Disease Duration, UPDRS, H&Y, Falls Efficacy Scale - International (FES-I), new Freezing of Gait Questionnaire (nFOGQ), and Levodopa Equivalent Daily Dose (LEDD) for both PwPD and HC groups.
The study did not control for day-to-day fluctuations in hours of sleep, stress, or caffeine intake, which are potential sources of variance in OMT frequency measurements.

The iTremor ONE device was used to measure OMT, and minor factors such as blinking, eye movement, or eyelid blocking occasionally impacted data acquisition, though repeated measurements within a session prevented data loss.

The OMT frequency range observed in the study was approximately 63-70Hz, which is lower than the 68-88Hz reported in a previous study, a difference potentially attributable to the iTremor ONE being more accurate than previous piezoelectric tools and the previous study's lack of detailed demographic or clinical data.
The study included 33 participants with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) and 31 healthy controls (HC), with PwPD participants having a mean age of 69.06 years and a mean disease duration of 5.08 years.

Participants with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) were assessed in both OFF and ON medication states, with the OFF group having a mean age of 67.37 years and the ON group having a mean age of 67.37 years, while the healthy control group had a mean age of 67.32 years.

The study utilized the MDS-UPDRS motor subsection to assess clinical symptoms, specifically correlating OMT frequency with item 3.1 (speech) and facial items, and used the Hoehn & Yahr scale to stage disease severity.
Cognitive function was measured using the MoCA, Trail Making Test A and B, CLOX1, CLOX2, JLO, and Forward digit span, while visual function was assessed via Visual Acuity and Contrast Sensitivity.

The study calculated intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) for OMT measurements across Visit 1 and Visit 2, with values of .94 (.86-.98) for the right eye, .93 (.82-.97) for the left eye, and .92 (.81-.967) for both eyes.
Diagnostic value was assessed using ROC curve analysis and Area Under the Curve (AUC), which yielded an AUC of 0.745-0.773 for OMT in distinguishing between PwPD and HC groups.
The study used a standard 12-hour washout period to test OMT frequency in the 'OFF' medication state, comparing it to the 'ON' state measured 1 hour after anti-Parkinson's medication consumption.

The previous study referenced used the subjective Webster Scale bradykinesia section to categorize patients into 'ON' or 'OFF' groups instead of a medication washout period, which reflects disease severity rather than medication effects on OMT.
In the single patient case where dopaminergic medication was withdrawn for 48 hours, OMT frequency was recorded as 78.5Hz at 24 hours 'ON' and 66.5Hz at 48 hours 'OFF'.
The current study's PwPD and healthy older adult OMT frequency readings ranged from approximately 63-70Hz.
The previous OMT study in PwPD utilized a longer washout period than the standard 12 hours due to an ongoing medical investigation of the patient involved.
The study consisted of a homogeneous mild-to-moderate Parkinson's disease cohort (Hoehn and Yahr stage II-III) with no stratification by Parkinson's disease phenotype or disease duration.
The study was conducted within the North East of England, which may limit generalisability to more diverse populations and geographic regions.
Factors such as caffeine intake, sleep quality, and home environment were not formally recorded and should be controlled for in future studies.

Analyses were limited to univariate correlational and group comparison approaches, with future studies recommended to employ multivariable modelling to better account for potential confounding variables.

The study's cumulative sleep debt calculation relies on specific scoring algorithms and software versions that are currently undocumented, creating a methodological blocker for verifying the reaction time numbers.

The ocular microtremor study utilized a standard 12-hour washout protocol for the 'OFF' state and reported test-retest ICCs over 0.90, but failed to formally record confounders such as caffeine intake and sleep quality.
The study was designed as a randomized controlled trial to evaluate the effectiveness of body weight-supported treadmill training on gait performance in individuals with Parkinson's disease.
The study design involved 40 patients with idiopathic Parkinson's disease who were randomly assigned to an experimental group (n=20) or a control group (n=20).
The experimental group received gait training with a lower-body positive pressure treadmill, while the control group underwent conventional physiotherapy.
Both the experimental group and the control group trained twice weekly for 4 months.
Outcomes were assessed at baseline (T0) and post-intervention (T1), with primary outcomes classified as gait speed, step length, balance, and postural stability.
Secondary outcomes assessed included quality of life, fear of falling, and anxiety.

The study was an exploratory pilot randomized controlled trial with 40 patients diagnosed with Parkinson's Disease who had a Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) score of 81 or less, enrolled from the Parkinson's Outpatient Clinic at IRCCS Centro Neurolesi "Bonino-Pulejo" in Messina, Italy, between May 2021 and March 2023. An a priori sample size calculation was not performed for this trial.

Participants were included if they met the Movement Disorder Society Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Parkinson's Disease, had evidence of freezing of gait, were aged 50 to 85 years, had a Hoehn and Yahr stage between II and III, had an age- and education-corrected Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE) score of 24 or higher, and had no musculoskeletal disorders, visual or auditory impairments, or cardiovascular or pulmonary diseases.

Participants were excluded if they had a diagnosis of parkinsonism according to the Movement Disorder Society Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Parkinson's Disease, had a pacemaker or infusion systems such as Duodopa gel via J-Peg system, had comorbidities contraindicating physical exercise, or had severe visual or auditory impairment.

Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to the Experimental Group (n=20) or Control Group (n=20) using a computer-generated simple random sequence from random.org, without stratification or block randomization procedures. Blinding of patients and therapists was not feasible, but all outcome assessments were performed by evaluators blinded to group allocation.
The study was approved by the Local Ethics Committee of IRCCS Centro Neurolesi "Bonino Pulejo" (U224/22), and all participants provided signed informed consent.

Forty patients were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to the experimental group (n=20) or the control group (n=20) after 5 of 45 assessed patients were excluded, with no losses to follow-up or discontinuations occurring.

Both the experimental and control groups underwent 20 sessions of 60-minute gait training twice a week for 4 months, supervised by two physiotherapists, with treadmill settings at a zero-degree incline and participants walking barefoot.

The experimental group used the AlterG anti-gravity treadmill model M320 (AlterG, Inc., Fremont, CA, USA) with a 60% body weight reduction applied during each session, while the control group used a conventional treadmill.

Initial treadmill speeds were based on baseline gait analysis and were gradually increased over the 20 sessions to reach each participant's maximum walking capacity while ensuring proper gait performance.

The experimental group underwent gait training using the AlterG anti-gravity treadmill model M320 (AlterG, Inc., Fremont, CA, USA), which utilizes lower-body positive pressure (LBPP) technology to provide body weight support from 20% to 100% of body weight in 1% increments.

Postural stability was evaluated using the Zebris Medical GmbH pressure-sensitive platform, recording Center of Pressure (CoP) length, average velocity, 95% confidence ellipse, and load distribution while patients stood still with eyes open and closed for 10 seconds.

Gait parameters were analyzed at T0 and T1 using the BTS Gaitlab system, which is equipped with motion capture systems, force platforms, and electromyographic sensors, following the DAVIS protocol for reflective markers and EMG sensors.

The study applied surface EMG electrodes to major lower-limb muscles and extracted electromyography data for the timing of activation and deactivation of the tibialis anterior, gastrocnemius, quadriceps, and hamstrings.
The statistical analysis used the open-source R software package version 4.2.2 with a 95% confidence level and a 5% alpha error, setting statistical significance at p<0.05.
The researchers did not analyze raw change scores (Δ=T1-T0) because these metrics are known to inflate error variance in small samples, which introduces a methodological bias.
The study authors noted that given the small sample size and multiple endpoints, the calculated p-values must be interpreted with caution.

The study sample consisted of 40 subjects, divided into an experimental group (EG) of 20 subjects and a control group (CG) of 20 subjects. The global sample included 30 males (75%) and 10 females (25%), with a mean age of 67.18 ± 7.29 years.

The experimental group (EG) had a mean age of 68.5 ± 7.75 years and a mean disease duration of 9 ± 8.5 years, while the control group (CG) had a mean age of 65.9 ± 6.73 years and a mean disease duration of 12.5 ± 7.5 years.

Primary motor outcomes were measured at T0 (baseline) and T1 (post-treatment), with data presented as means ± standard deviations for normally distributed variables and medians (first and third quartiles) for non-normally distributed variables.
Statistical significance was set at p<0.05, and the authors noted that p-values must be interpreted with caution due to the small sample size and multiple endpoints.

The study utilized the BTS Gait Lab (BTS Bioengineering, Milan, Italy), which includes infrared cameras, force plates, and wireless electromyographic sensors, to perform quantitative gait analysis at baseline (T0) and after treatment (T1).

Data acquisition followed the DAVIS multifactorial protocol, which combines kinematic, kinetic, and electromyographic assessments, with reflective markers placed on standard anatomical landmarks and surface EMG electrodes applied to major lower-limb muscles.
Each participant in the experimental group performed standing and walking trials at a self-selected comfortable speed.
The gait analysis recorded parameters including cadence, step width, step length, stance and swing phases, average speed, Gait Deviation Index (GDI), and Gait Profile Score (GPS).
The study analyzed the stance phase (60% of the gait cycle) and swing phase (40%) for stability and efficiency, while cadence, step width, and step length were used to assess walking performance.

Secondary outcomes were assessed using the Falls Efficacy Scale International (FES-I), a 16-item questionnaire with scores ranging from 16 to 64, and the Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire-39 (PDQ-39), which consists of 39 items scored on a 5-point Likert scale from 0 to 4 and transformed into a 0-100 scale.

The Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A), a 14-item clinician-administered tool, was used to assess anxiety severity, with each item scored on a 5-point scale from 0 to 4, resulting in a total score range of 0 to 56.
The statistical analysis utilized a paired Student's t-test for parametric data, a Wilcoxon signed rank test for nonparametric data, and a Mann-Whitney U test for nonparametric comparisons.
The study measured specific gait parameters including Cadence, Average Gait Speed, Stride width, Gait Deviation Index Right/Left, Gait Profile Score Right/Left, and Step Length Right/Left.

The study utilized a control group design where the control group did not show significant improvements between T0 and T1, allowing the researchers to attribute the observed changes in the experimental group to the intervention.
The study conducted correlation analysis to explore the relationship between patient-reported outcomes and instrumented gait measures within the experimental group.
The study employed gait training with body weight support through differential air pressure as the intervention method.

Figure 2 presents a comparison between baseline (T0) and follow-up (T1) values in the experimental group for gait and balance variables, where bars represent the median and error bars indicate the interquartile range (IQR).

The study utilized Spearman's rank correlation analysis to examine relationships between clinical outcomes and gait/balance parameters, with significance thresholds set at p<0.05, p<0.01, and p<0.001.
The study design was an exploratory pilot trial, and the authors note that a repeated-measures analysis was not feasible for the statistical tests applied.
The study utilized a sample size of n=20 per group, which the authors note limits generalizability, and the trial was conducted with an exploratory nature that increases the risk of Type I error.
The study assessed multiple endpoints but was not feasible for a repeated-measures analysis, and appropriate statistical tests were applied to the data.

The study employed the LLBP therapy treadmill, which allows for precise, incremental unloading of body weight while preserving natural gait kinematics to facilitate safer and more controlled gait training.

Statistical analysis of the secondary outcomes utilized the paired Student's t-test for parametric tests, the Wilcoxon signed rank test for nonparametric tests, and the Mann-Whitney U test for nonparametric tests.

The study's reliability is compromised by the absence of specific firmware versions and sensor calibration logs for the iTremor ONE device, which prevents verification of whether the 70-150Hz frequency range was adjusted for ambient light conditions.

The high inter-class correlation coefficients (ICCs) cannot be validated for real-world use because the specific algorithm parameters used to filter 70-150Hz oscillations from standard video noise are missing from the provided data.

The claim of high reliability is undermined by the study's moderate diagnostic accuracy, indicated by an Area Under the Curve (AUC) value under 0.78, which suggests a significant error rate for individual patients that is not adequately addressed in the methodological reporting.

The study utilized competing risk analysis and Cox regression to analyze the relationship between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease, accounting for antipsychotic medication exposure and comorbid conditions.

Researchers accessed confidential National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) data through the NHIS Data Sharing Service website, with access granted only for a predefined period approved for each research project.

The study was a retrospective cohort design using a customized database from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) of South Korea that included patients diagnosed with schizophrenia and matched controls. The analysis involved propensity score matching adjusted for demographic, clinical, and comorbidity variables, followed by competing risk analysis and Cox regression to evaluate the relationship between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease.

The de-identified claims data used in the study were obtained from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) of Korea and are not publicly available due to NHIS data protection regulations and internal data-use policies.

The study was a retrospective cohort study designed to evaluate the risk of Parkinson's disease associated with schizophrenia and the influence of antipsychotic medications prescribed at the time of schizophrenia diagnosis on Parkinson's disease development.

The study was a retrospective cohort study using a customized database from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) of South Korea, covering data from 2010 to 2021, with data accessed on July 11, 2022. Schizophrenia was defined by ICD-10 code F2* requiring one inpatient record or two outpatient records within one year, and patients diagnosed in 2010 or under 18 years of age were excluded to define incident new cases.

Patients with schizophrenia were matched with patients without schizophrenia using propensity score matching in a 1:2 ratio based on the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) score, age, gender, and index year. The matching used a caliper width of 0.2 standard deviations of the logit of the propensity score, with a standardized mean difference of ≥ 0.1 indicating imbalance, and the CCI score was calculated from records one year prior to the index date.

All statistical analyses were performed using SAS Enterprise Guide version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA), with a two-sided confidence interval of 0.05 considered to indicate statistical significance.

The study utilized de-identified secondary data provided by the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS), and all analyses were conducted within the NHIS-controlled secure research environment with restricted access to ensure data security and privacy.
Access to the data was available only through the designated NHIS analysis center, and remote access from personal computers or external networks was not permitted.
A total of 42,522 patients with schizophrenia were matched to 85,041 controls by age, gender, matching-period Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) score, and index year.

The outcome of incident Parkinson's disease was defined as a new diagnosis using the ICD-10 code G20 occurring at least one year after the initial schizophrenia diagnosis, requiring at least one inpatient diagnosis or two outpatient diagnoses with the G20 code within a one-year period to minimize diagnostic errors.

Cox regression analysis was used to calculate the crude and adjusted hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals for Parkinson's disease incidence rates, and survival analysis was performed using the Kaplan-Meier method with significance based on the log-rank test.
Fine-Gray's competing risk analysis was used to determine the risk of Parkinson's disease while considering death as a competing risk factor.
Sensitivity analysis was conducted using data from 1, 2, or 3 years before the end date to account for limited knowledge about the onset of Parkinson's disease in schizophrenia patients.

The relationship between antipsychotic medications and Parkinson's disease development was investigated using the intent-to-treat method, performing Cox regression, Kaplan-Meier analysis, and log-rank tests based on medications prescribed at the time of the initial diagnosis.

Covariates for the study were based on records from one year prior to the outcome and included demographic factors, clinical conditions, the Charlson Comorbidity Index, mental disorders (ICD-10, F00-F69), and related medications (ATC, N05A-N06D).

The study excluded variables with a phi coefficient of 0.4 or higher, including CCI score, medication N05A-N06D, mood (affective) disorders, and hyperlipidemia, to ensure the reliability of the multivariable analysis.

In cases of high collinearity between two diseases, the disease with more associations with other variables was excluded, while in cases of collinearity between a disease and a medication, the medication was excluded.
After excluding collinear variables and adjusting for the remaining factors, the study utilized competing risk analysis to evaluate the association between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease risk.
The study employed Cox proportional regression and Fine-Gray competing risk analysis to calculate crude and adjusted hazard ratios for Parkinson's disease.

The multivariate analysis adjusted for variables including schizophrenia, sex, age, Charlson Comorbidity Index, and specific comorbidities such as mood disorders, neurotic disorders, and coronary heart disease.

The analysis included medication types categorized by ATC codes, specifically N05A (Antipsychotics), N05B (Anxiolytics), N05C (Hypnotics and sedatives), N06A (Antidepressants), N06B (Psychostimulants for ADHD), and N06D (Anti-dementia drugs).

The study utilized a large retrospective cohort derived from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) database in South Korea to investigate the association between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease.
The statistical analysis employed both a no competing risk model and a Fine-Gray competing risk model to assess the association between exposure duration and Parkinson's disease risk.
Variables with a Phi correlation coefficient greater than 0.4 were excluded from the adjusted hazard ratio analysis to manage multicollinearity.
Kaplan-Meier analysis was performed to evaluate event-free survival for Parkinson's disease among users of specific antipsychotic medications compared to non-users.

The study included a control group of 85,041 participants and a schizophrenia patient group of 42,522 participants, with baseline matching resulting in a mean age of 66.36 ± 18.27 years for the control group and 66.26 ± 18.48 years for the schizophrenia group. The mean index year for both groups was 2016.2, and the mean follow-up duration was 4.03 ± 2.98 years for the control group and 2.85 ± 2.77 years for the schizophrenia group.

A sensitivity analysis incorporating competing risk analysis was performed to confirm the robustness of the adjusted hazard ratio for Parkinson's disease across 1-, 2-, and 3-year periods of comorbidities. A Kaplan-Meier plot was used to assess Parkinson's disease-free survival rates during the follow-up period, with a log-rank test yielding a P-value of <0.0001.

Multivariate analysis was conducted to evaluate the association between antipsychotic drug use (ATC code N05A) and the development of Parkinson's disease, yielding a hazard ratio of 1.076 with a 95% confidence interval of 1.023-1.132 and a p-value of 0.0045.

The study defined Parkinson's disease as new diagnoses made at least one year after the initial schizophrenia diagnosis to minimize the misclassification of transient, drug-related parkinsonian symptoms as idiopathic Parkinson's disease.

The study applied a one-year lag period between the initial schizophrenia diagnosis and the Parkinson's disease diagnosis as a conservative methodological approach to reduce the possibility that early, reversible medication-induced parkinsonism was misclassified as true degenerative Parkinson's disease.
The study utilized Kaplan-Meier plots to analyze Event-Free Survival for Parkinson's Disease, stratified by schizophrenia status and by antipsychotic drug prescription.

The study performed adjusted Hazard Ratio (HR) analyses for Parkinson's Disease in patients prescribed antipsychotic drugs, controlling for variables including age, sex, organic mental disorders, substance use disorders, neurotic disorders, gastric disease, osteoarthritis, head injury, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes mellitus, hypertensive disease, end-stage renal disease, coronary heart disease, and cerebrovascular disease.

The study performed adjusted Hazard Ratio (HR) analyses for Parkinson's Disease in patients prescribed quetiapine or risperidone, controlling for variables including age, sex, organic mental disorders, substance use disorders, neurotic disorders, gastric disease, osteoarthritis, head injury, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes mellitus, hypertensive disease, end-stage renal disease, coronary heart disease, and cerebrovascular disease.

The study utilized a retrospective observational design and a large-scale administrative database, which restricted access to granular clinical information such as disease severity, symptom onset timing, and neuroimaging results like DaTscan. The administrative claims data framework also made it challenging to reflect individual daily dosing ranges or the exact cumulative duration of exposure, limiting the pharmacological interpretation of medication associations.

To improve diagnostic accuracy and mitigate misclassification based on administrative codes, the study defined diseases as requiring at least one inpatient record or two outpatient records within a year. The absence of laboratory test results and the lack of a multicenter design are identified as limitations that may restrict the generalizability of the findings.

The study applied an intent-to-treat approach to mitigate the limitation that medication adherence could not be directly assessed. While multiple comparisons across different antipsychotic agents were not explicitly adjusted, potential confounding was addressed by incorporating a wide range of clinical and demographic covariates into the multivariate models.

A competing risk analysis was conducted to account for the potential impact of premature death before Parkinson's disease onset, with results consistent with the standard analysis without competing risks. The analysis focused on drugs with larger sample sizes, so individual analyses for all medications were not performed.

The study utilized a cohort design with competing risk adjustment and specifically focused on schizophrenia patients while including a wide range of covariates and adjusting for comorbidities and medication use.
The study applied an intent-to-treat approach to mitigate the limitation that medication adherence could not be directly assessed.

The study conducted a collinearity analysis to reduce confounding effects by excluding highly correlated variables, though residual bias may persist due to the close association between schizophrenia diagnosis and antipsychotic medication use.
The study included a 1-year lag period to address the risk of reverse causation, although this bias cannot be entirely dismissed given the long prodromal phase of Parkinson's disease.
The study performed a focused comparison of two antipsychotic medications to explore their differential impacts on Parkinson's disease risk.
The study evaluated the association of schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease using a large claims data including the majority of the Korean population.

The diagnostic performance of the OMT frequency biomarker, characterized by an AUC of 0.760 and a sensitivity of 0.606, is methodologically compromised by the absence of a specified multiple comparisons correction for covariates, which inflates the Type I error risk and prevents the calculation of a valid 95% confidence interval without the exact sample size per group.

Verification of the 70-150Hz signal filtering is currently impossible due to missing code parameters and software versions, as well as unspecified webcam distance and calibration logs, which are critical for assessing the robustness of the AUC of 0.760 under variable ambient light conditions.

The rehabilitation study's protocol for determining baseline treadmill speeds and the exact unloading percentages used across the 20 sessions are undocumented, preventing verification of the differential air pressure effects. Reproducing the body weight support calculations requires the specific Rysen system logs and precise software versions, which are currently missing from the documentation.

The microtremor paper's clinical validation group has a sample size of n=33, a parameter that is barely sufficient to distinguish the Area Under the Curve (AUC) from chance. The rehabilitation study's small cohorts lack a reported 95% confidence interval for the gait speed effect size, limiting the statistical power of the kinematic claims.

The treadmill study's validity is compromised by the absence of a priori sample size calculation, which renders the reported 'excellent' agreement and gait improvements potentially driven by chance rather than the intervention itself due to an underpowered, exploratory design.

The ICC(2,1) > 0.90 metric is conditional on unspecified environmental controls and lacks the exact n per group and 95% confidence intervals required to determine if the 'excellent' agreement is a statistical artifact of a small denominator.

The systematic absence of reported 95% confidence intervals for primary effect sizes across all three studies precludes any assessment of the precision of the estimates, leaving the distinction between meaningful effects and noise fundamentally unverified.

The 70-150Hz signal processing methodology is methodologically opaque due to the absence of raw data, specific software versions, and calibration logs, which prevents verification of the high test-retest reliability claims.

The device's diagnostic utility is compromised by a lack of evidence confirming that results remain stable outside the specific controlled 12-hour washout protocol, as the necessary calibration logs to test this boundary condition are missing.

Reproducibility of the primary ANOVA and unadjusted ICC(2,1) calculations is fundamentally limited because the exact sample size per group is not provided, preventing independent verification of whether the observed agreement is a statistical artifact of a small denominator.

The absence of reported 95% confidence intervals for the reliability estimates prevents independent verification of the precision of the statistical metrics, leaving the robustness of the agreement unverified.
