The study utilized the iTremor ONE device provided by Head Diagnostics to measure ocular microtremor (OMT) non-invasively using safe laser technology.
The OMT measurement process using the handheld device takes three seconds and is non-invasive.

The study data is pseudo-anonymised and cannot be publicly deposited because it was collected from NHS patients under ethics approval REF: 23/WM/0004 and Northumbria University ethics Project No. 0034.
The study used the iTremor ONE hand-held device to measure ocular microtremor (OMT) in 33 participants with Parkinson's Disease and 31 age-matched healthy controls.
Analytical validation for OMT measurement involved a test-retest reliability assessment on 22 participants with Parkinson's Disease, evaluated using interclass correlation coefficients (ICC).

Clinical validation compared OMT frequency in 33 participants with Parkinson's Disease to controls and tested 24 participants with Parkinson's Disease in 'OFF' (12-hour withdrawal) and 'ON' states of anti-Parkinson's dopaminergic medication.

The iTremor ONE device from Head Diagnostics Ltd. in Dublin, Ireland, uses laser technology to measure ocular motor tremor (OMT) and is described as a high-resolution, non-invasive, compact, and portable technique.

A critical gap in the literature exists because no study has yet examined ocular motor tremor (OMT) using a non-invasive, portable technique in a clinical Parkinson's disease population, which has prevented OMT from being evaluated as a clinically viable biomarker.

The iTremor ONE device has not yet undergone analytical and clinical validation to determine whether it is accurate, reliable, and sensitive to clinical groups of interest, such as Parkinson's disease.

Ocular microtremor (OMT) oscillates at a frequency range of 70-150Hz in healthy subjects and cannot be detected by the naked eye or standard video-based eye-tracking systems due to insufficient sensitivity.

Existing invasive OMT measurement techniques, including piezoelectric strain gauges, fixed contact lens accelerometers, and eyelid fixed accelerometers, require eye anaesthetisation, highly trained operators, and constant uninterrupted scleral contact for up to 60 minutes, which introduces unknown loading effects and limits validation of new techniques.

There is no gold standard technique for measuring ocular microtremor (OMT), resulting in variable application of measurement protocols and limited generalisability of underlying deficit interpretations.
The full protocol for the study is published at https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0313452.
The study used the iTremor ONE device to measure OMT frequency in Hz.
The study was registered with Clinicaltrials.gov under identifier NCT06051877.
The study received NHS Research Ethics Committee approval under reference 23/WM/0004 and an MHRA letter of no objection under reference CI/2023/0031/GB.
Participants with Parkinson's disease were included if they met UK brain bank criteria for diagnosis.
Healthy controls were aged 50 years old or above.
Participants were excluded if they had a MoCA score of less than 21.

The iTremor ONE device (Head Diagnostics Ltd., Dublin, Ireland, software version 0.19) measures ocular motor tremor (OMT) by recording angular displacement via laser speckle correlation in the Fourier plane of a lens, using band-pass filtering to segregate OMT from other eye movements, hand movements, and head movements.

Test-retest reliability for ocular motor tremor (OMT) in people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) was assessed using 22 participants across two home-based visits exactly one week apart, conducted at the same time of day (within 30 minutes) and in the same location.

Disease severity in people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) was assessed in the "ON" state, one hour after Levodopa medication intake, using the Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson's disease Rating scale part III (UPDRS-III).

Ocular motor tremor (OMT) measurements required participants to sit in a high-backed chair with curtains or blinds closed to dim light, remove glasses or contact lenses, and maintain a relaxed gaze at a wall target at eye level for approximately 3 seconds per eye using a low-level laser directed at the sclera.

Ocular motor tremor (OMT) readings were repeated if the participant blinked, with three readings taken and averaged for each eye using a single iTremor ONE device operated by the same individual for every measurement.
The optimal cut-off point for outcome measures was determined as the point closest to the corner (0,1) with a false positive rate of 0% and sensitivity of 100% in the ROC plane.

Convergent validity analysis correlated OMT frequencies with demographic and clinical measures using Pearson's correlation for normally distributed data and Spearman's correlation for non-normally distributed data.
Paired t-tests were performed comparing 'ON' and 'OFF' medication groups to examine whether OMT reduces in the 'OFF' medication state in Parkinson's disease.
The analytical validation cohort included 22 people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) with mild to moderate disease severity and a mean MoCA score of approximately 27.

The clinical validation cohort included 33 people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) and 31 healthy controls (HC), with PwPD participants having mild to moderate disease severity and a mean MoCA score of approximately 27.

The response to known intervention cohort included 24 people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) with mild to moderate disease severity and mean MoCA scores of approximately 27 when 'OFF' medication and approximately 26 when 'ON' medication.
Test-retest reliability for OMT frequency (Hz) in people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) demonstrated excellent agreement with all Intraclass Correlation Coefficients (ICC) greater than 0.90.

The mean difference between OMT readings from first and second visits was 1.14 Hz for the right eye with Limits of Agreement (LoA) of 6.6%, 1.70 Hz for the left eye with LoA of 7.4%, and 1.73 Hz for both eyes with LoA of 7.5%.

OMT measurements were repeated by the examiner when the iTremor ONE device reported inability to take a reading, typically due to eye blinks, obstruction from eyelashes or eyelids, or changes in gaze direction.
The study used a single iTremor ONE device operated by the same trained operator for all OMT measurements to ensure consistency.
Clinical validation included data from 33 PwPD (22 assessed at home, 11 in the laboratory) and 31 healthy controls (HCs) assessed in the laboratory.

For the 24 PwPD assessed in the home environment, the 'OFF' medication state required a minimum of 12 hours without dopaminergic medication, followed by an 'ON' state assessment 60 minutes after taking the morning levodopa dose.
Participants were seated in a high-backed chair looking at a target at eye level, with room lighting controlled consistently and testing conducted in a quiet environment.
Three OMT readings per eye were averaged for each measurement.

Collected variables included age, gender, education, Falls Efficacy Scale (FES-I), visual acuity (LogMar), contrast sensitivity (LogCS), disease duration, MDS-UPDRS part III, Hoehn and Yahr stage, freezing of gait questionnaire (FOGQ), levodopa equivalent daily dose (LEDD), and hours since last dose.
Data analysis was performed using SPSS version 28 (IBM Inc, IL, USA).
Normal data distribution was confirmed using Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests and Shapiro-Wilk tests with a threshold of p > 0.05.

OMT frequency outcomes were assessed as an average for both eyes and separately for left and right eyes, with invalid readings treated as missing data and excluded from analysis using available case analysis.
Reliability was assessed using intra-class correlations (ICC2,1) with interpretation thresholds of poor <0.5, moderate 0.50-0.75, good 0.75-0.90, and excellent >0.90.
Known groups validity was examined using ANOVA with group (PwPD vs. HCs) as a between-subject factor, followed by Tukey post-hoc analysis and ROC curve analysis for each eye.

ROC analysis interpreted AUC as outstanding >0.9, excellent 0.8-0.9, good 0.7-0.8, fair 0.6-0.7, and fail <0.5, with the optimal cut-off point determined as the point closest to (0,1) with a false positive rate of 0% and sensitivity of 100%.
The study did not control for multiple comparison corrections such as Bonferroni.
The study utilized the iTremor ONE technology to measure ocular microtremor (OMT) frequency in Hz, achieving an Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) greater than 0.9 for frequency detection.
The iTremor ONE device employs a laser-speckle technique for OMT detection, which the authors suggest offers greater accuracy than previously employed OMT detection techniques.

No significant differences in ocular microtremor (OMT) readings were observed when participants were 'OFF' compared to 'ON' anti-Parkinson's medication, a finding consistent across right eye, left eye, and both eye readings.

The diagnostic performance of average ocular microtremor (OMT) frequency in differentiating People with Parkinson's Disease (PwPD) from Healthy Controls (HCs) is defined by specific Area Under the Curve (AUC) values, cut-off frequencies in Hertz, sensitivity, and 1-specificity for the right eye, left eye, and both eyes combined.

The study reports Pearson correlation coefficients (r) and p-values for the relationship between overall average OMT frequency and clinical measures including Age, Sex, Disease Duration, MDS Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale III (UPDRS), Hohen & Yahr Stage (H&Y), Falls Efficacy Scale-International (FES-I), new Freezing of Gait Questionnaire (nFOGQ), and Levodopa Equivalent Daily Dose (LEDD), separated by PwPD and HC groups.

Healthy controls (HC, n=31) displayed higher mean OMT frequency than participants with Parkinson's disease (PwPD, n=33) for the right eye (69.65 Hz vs 63.98 Hz), left eye (69.24 Hz vs 63.58 Hz), and both eyes (69.44 Hz vs 63.78 Hz), with Cohen's d effect sizes of 0.88, 1.09, and 0.99 respectively.
The diagnostic value of OMT assessment for PwPD versus HC was evaluated using ROC curve analysis, yielding an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.745-0.773.

In the PwPD group, lower OMT frequency in the right, left, and both eyes correlated with poorer speech (MDS-UPDRS item 3.1), with correlation coefficients of r=-.477 (p=.005), r=-.367 (p=.036), and r=-.432 (p=.012) respectively.
The study cohort included 31 healthy controls (12 male, 19 female) and 33 PwPD participants (19 male, 14 female), with mean ages of 67.32 years and 69.06 years respectively.

PwPD participants had a mean disease duration of 5.08 years and a mean UPDRS III score of 35.94, while the PwPD OFF subgroup (n=24) had a mean UPDRS III score of 36.96 and the PwPD ON subgroup (n=24) had a mean UPDRS III score of 31.91.

Test-retest reliability for OMT measures in PwPD showed Intraclass Correlation Coefficients (ICC) of 0.94 (95% CI 0.86-0.98) for the right eye, 0.93 (95% CI 0.82-0.97) for the left eye, and 0.92 (95% CI 0.81-0.967) for both eyes.
The study used a standard 12-hour washout period to test OMT frequency in the 'OFF' state compared to 1 hour after anti-Parkinson's medication consumption in the 'ON' state.

A previous study reported OMT frequency values of 78.5 Hz for a patient 24 hours after medication and 66.5 Hz after a 48-hour medication withdrawal, which exceeded the 63-70 Hz range observed in the current study's PwPD and healthy older adult groups.
The current study detected no difference in OMT frequency between the 'ON' and 'OFF' dopaminergic medication states using a 12-hour washout period.

The iTremor ONE device demonstrated good discriminative ability for differentiating PwPD from HCs with an AUC of 0.75-0.77 and Cohen's d values of 0.88-1.09. The OMT frequency range across PwPD and HCs was approximately 63-70Hz, which is lower than the 68-88Hz range reported in a previous study using piezoelectric tools, a difference potentially attributable to the higher accuracy of the iTremor ONE.

The difference in OMT frequency readings between the first and second assessments was between 1.13-1.72Hz, representing 1.74-2.69% of the average measures. This variability was not controlled for factors such as hours of sleep, stress, caffeine intake, medication, fatigue, or disease 'ON' and 'OFF' periods, and requires investigation in a larger population to establish expected day-to-day variation.

No adverse events occurred during the study, and no participants withdrew. Minor factors such as blinking, eye movement, and eyelid or lash blocking impacted the ability to obtain OMT measurements, but repeated measurements within the session prevented data loss.

The study cohort consisted of patients with Parkinson's disease at Hoehn & Yahr stage II-III without stratification by PD phenotype (e.g., tremor-dominant vs. akinetic-rigid subtypes) or disease duration, and was conducted exclusively in the North East of England.

Confounding factors including caffeine intake, sleep quality, and home environment were not formally recorded, and statistical analyses were limited to univariate correlational and group comparison approaches rather than multivariable modelling.

The study provides analytical and clinical validation evidence for the iTremor ONE device, which was used to non-invasively measure OMT frequency in patients with Parkinson's disease and healthy controls.
Supporting information includes S1 Table listing missing cases and S1 Fig containing Bland Altman Plots, both provided as DOCX files.

The ocular microtremor study requires the specific controlled washout protocols to verify if the biomarker's precision holds outside the lab; without these exact protocol parameters, the claim of viable home monitoring is not replicable.

The sleep debt study's claim of equivalence to intoxication is blocked by the lack of a causal bridge between the measured reaction time data and real-world driving safety, meaning the specific overreach in the authors' claim cannot be replicated as a factual finding without additional evidence.

Replication of the 'daily life' impact claims is blocked until the acquisition parameters and sample size of the first paper are established, as sloppy methodological details render the translation from lab metrics to real-world outcomes non-reproducible.
Data for the study are available from the Ethics Committee (contact via 09060128109) for researchers who meet the criteria for access to confidential data.

The study utilized a lower-body positive pressure treadmill (Alter-G) for the experimental group and conventional physiotherapy for the control group, with both groups training twice weekly for 4 months.
The study involved forty patients with idiopathic Parkinson's disease, randomly assigned to an experimental group (n=20) or a control group (n=20).

Outcomes were assessed at baseline (T0) and post-intervention (T1), with primary outcomes including gait speed, step length, balance, and postural stability, and secondary outcomes including quality of life, fear of falling, and anxiety.

The study utilizes an Anti-Gravity Treadmill, specifically the Alter-G device, which uses differential air pressure technology to reduce body weight during ambulation for gait training in Parkinson's disease patients.

The primary outcomes for the randomized controlled trial are gait performance, freezing of gait episodes, and gait cycle quality, while secondary outcomes include cadence, step length, walking speed, pain, mood, and overall quality of life.

The experimental group underwent gait training using the AlterG anti-gravity treadmill model M320 (AlterG, Inc., Fremont, CA, USA), which uses lower-body positive pressure technology to adjust support from 20% to 100% of body weight in 1% increments.

Postural stability was evaluated using the Zebris Medical GmbH platform, a pressure-sensitive system that records Center of Pressure length, average velocity, 95% confidence ellipse, and load distribution while patients stood still with eyes open and closed for 10 seconds.

Gait parameters were analyzed at T0 and T1 using the BTS Gaitlab system, which is equipped with motion capture systems, force platforms, and electromyographic sensors, following the DAVIS protocol with reflective markers and EMG sensors.
The experimental group underwent gait training using the AlterG anti-gravity treadmill model M320 (AlterG, Inc., Fremont, CA, USA) with a 60% body weight reduction applied during each session.

The rehabilitation program consisted of 20 sessions (2 times a week for 4 months), with each session lasting approximately 60 minutes and comprising a 15-minute warm-up, treadmill training at a zero-degree incline, and a 15-minute cooldown.
Treadmill speeds were initially based on baseline gait analysis and were gradually increased over the 20 sessions to reach each participant's maximum walking capacity.
The study was approved by the Local Ethics Committee of IRCCS Centro Neurolesi "Bonino Pulejo" (approval code U224/22), and participants provided signed informed consent.

The study enrolled 40 patients with Parkinson's Disease from the Parkinson's Outpatient Clinic at IRCCS Centro Neurolesi "Bonino-Pulejo" in Messina, Italy, between May 2021 and March 2023 under Clinical Trial registration NCT0574025.

Inclusion criteria required a diagnosis of Parkinson's Disease per Movement Disorder Society Clinical Diagnostic Criteria, evidence of Freezing of Gait, age 50-85 years, Hoehn and Yahr stage II-III, and a Mini Mental State Examination score of 24 or higher.

Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to an Experimental Group (n=20) receiving body weight-supported treadmill training with differential air pressure or a Control Group (n=20) receiving traditional physical exercise, using a computer-generated simple random sequence from random.org.
The study utilized R version 4.2.2 for statistical analysis, setting a 95% confidence level and a statistical significance threshold of p<0.05.
Surface EMG electrodes were applied to the tibialis anterior, gastrocnemius, quadriceps, and hamstrings muscles to record activation and deactivation timing.

The gait analysis protocol extracted kinematic data for hip, knee, ankle, and pelvic joint angles, kinetic data for joint moments and powers, and spatiotemporal parameters including cadence, step width, step length, stance and swing phases, and gait speed.
The Gait Deviation Index (GDI) and Gait Profile Score (GPS) were calculated as indices of gait quality during standing and walking trials performed at a self-selected comfortable speed.

Normality of continuous data was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test, with parametric tests (Student's t-test) used for normally distributed data and non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney U or Wilcoxon signed rank) for non-normally distributed data.

The study did not analyze raw change scores (Delta = T1 - T0) due to known inflation of error variance in small samples, but used Delta to calculate Spearman's rank correlations between quality of life, gait analysis scores, and motor scale.

The quantitative gait analysis utilized the BTS Gait Lab system (BTS Bioengineering, Milan, Italy), which includes infrared cameras, force plates, and wireless electromyographic sensors. Data acquisition followed the DAVIS multifactorial protocol, which combines kinematic, kinetic, and electromyographic assessments.

Reflective markers were placed on standard anatomical landmarks, and surface EMG electrodes were applied to major lower-limb muscles during the gait analysis. Each participant performed standing and walking trials at a self-selected comfortable speed.

The Falls Efficacy Scale International (FES-I) is a 16-item questionnaire with scores ranging from a minimum of 16 to a maximum of 64. The Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire-39 (PDQ-39) consists of 39 items grouped into eight domains, where each item is scored on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 0 to 4 and domain scores are transformed to a 0-100 scale.

The Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A) consists of 14 items, each scored on a 5-point scale ranging from 0 to 4, with a total score range of 0 to 56. The EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D) is a standardized generic instrument used to measure health-related quality of life.
The study utilized the Rysen system for body weight-supported treadmill training, which allows for precise, incremental unloading of body weight while preserving natural gait kinematics.
The sample size for the experimental and control groups was n=20 per group, and the trial was of an exploratory nature, which limits generalizability and increases the risk of Type I error.
A repeated-measures analysis was not feasible for the study due to the assessment of multiple endpoints, despite the application of appropriate statistical tests.
Data for normally distributed variables were presented as means±standard deviations, while data for non-normally distributed variables were presented as medians with first and third quartiles.
The statistical tests used were the paired Student's t-test for parametric data, the Wilcoxon signed rank test for nonparametric data, and the Mann-Whitney U test for nonparametric data.

The specific outcome measures included the Falls Efficacy Scale International (FES-I), EuroQol-5 Dimensions (EQ-5D), Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A), and the Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire - 39 items (PDQ-39).
The full correlation matrix results are provided in Supplementary S1 Fig and Table 3 of the document.

The statistical significance thresholds for the differences shown in Figure 2 are defined as *p<0.05 and **p<0.01.

The study sample consisted of 40 subjects (20 in the Experimental Group and 20 in the Control Group) with a mean age of 67.18 ± 7.29 years and a mean disease duration of 12 ± 8 years.
Statistical significance was set at p<0.05 with a 5% alpha error, and p-values must be interpreted with caution due to the small sample size and multiple endpoints.

Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics for the Experimental Group and Control Group are reported in Tables 1 and 2, with no significant differences found in age (p=0.25), sex distribution (p=0.99), or education level (p=0.99).

Significant baseline differences were observed in PDQ-39 subdomains Mobility (p=0.01), Cognition (p=0.01), and Communication (p=0.03), as well as in the 10-Min Walk Test (p<0.001), gait parameters Stance Phase Right/Left, Swing Phase Right/Left, and Gait Speed (all p<0.001), and Gait Deviation Index Left (p=0.02).
At T1, the Experimental Group showed greater improvement in EQ5-D (p=0.005), Mobility (p=0.007), and Communication (p<0.001) compared to the Control Group.

At T1, significant differences in motor performance were observed between the Experimental Group and Control Group for FES-I (p<0.001), 10-MWT (p<0.001), TUG Right, TUG Left, BBS (p<0.001), UPDRS-III (p<0.001), HY (p<0.001), and 6-MWT (p<0.001).
Table 2 presents primary motor outcomes at T0 and T1 as means ± standard deviations for normally distributed variables and medians (first and third quartiles) for non-normally distributed variables.

The 10-Min Walk Test (10MWT) values at T0 were 5.7 (5.3-7.8) for the Experimental Group and 5.6 (5.0-7.4) for the Control Group, and at T1 were 5.8 (4.2-6.4) for the Experimental Group and 5.6 (5.0-7.4) for the Control Group.

The Timed Up and Go test (TUG) values at T0 were 12.3 (10.1-14.7) for the Experimental Group and 11.3 (8.9-13.4) for the Control Group for the right side, and 12.9 (9.6-15.2) for the Experimental Group and 11.1 (9.6-13.2) for the Control Group for the left side.

The Berg Balance Scale (BBS) values at T0 were 47.5 (36.5-50.2) for the Experimental Group and 44.0 (40.0-47.2) for the Control Group, and at T1 were 50.0 (44.0-54.0) for the Experimental Group and 44.0 (40.0-47.2) for the Control Group.

The 6-Minute Walk Test (6MWT) values at T0 were 300.0 ± 75.6 for the Experimental Group and 280.0 (217.5-306.7) for the Control Group, and at T1 were 343.7 ± 87.3 for the Experimental Group and 280.0 (217.5-306.7) for the Control Group.

The Timed Sit-to-Stand test (TS-B) values at T0 were 14.0 (12.5-15.0) for the Experimental Group and 12.0 (10.0-14.0) for the Control Group, and at T1 were 15.0 (13.7-16.0) for the Experimental Group and 12.0 (10.0-14.0) for the Control Group.

The Timed Gait test (TS-G) values at T0 were 9.0 (7.0-10.2) for the Experimental Group and 8.0 (6.7-10.0) for the Control Group, and at T1 were 10.0 (8.7-11.0) for the Experimental Group and 8.0 (6.7-10.0) for the Control Group.

The study provides a Spearman's rank correlation matrix in S1 Fig, defining specific abbreviations for gait and balance parameters such as Average Gait Speed (AGS), Gait Deviation Index (GDI), Gait Profile Score (GPS), Step Length (SL), and Center of Pressure path length (COPL). The supporting information includes a SPIRIT checklist in S1 File and the full study protocol in S2 File, both available in PDF or TIFF formats.

The study concludes that body weight-supported treadmill training through differential air pressure improved primary outcomes including gait speed, step length, balance, and postural stability in patients with Parkinson's disease. The authors identify a gap in the current evidence, noting that larger randomized controlled trials with long-term follow-up are required to validate these preliminary findings and establish long-term effects.

The study's cross-sectional design comparing patients to controls without randomization prevents isolating the dopaminergic effect from baseline group differences, and the unspecified ambient light conditions and lack of reference standard calibration for the iTremor ONE sensor block verification of whether the high ICCs are genuine or artifacts of a static test environment.

The acquisition protocol fails to specify how ambient light or sensor calibration was controlled during the 70-150Hz signal extraction, meaning the video acquisition and filtering steps are undefined, which invalidates the assumption that the pipeline is robust for uncontrolled home environments.

The de-identified claims data used in the study were obtained from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) of Korea and are not publicly available due to NHIS data protection regulations and internal data-use policies.
The retrospective cohort study utilized a customized database from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) of South Korea containing patients diagnosed with schizophrenia and matched controls.

The study design is a retrospective cohort study evaluating the risk of Parkinson's disease associated with schizophrenia and the influence of antipsychotic medications prescribed at the time of schizophrenia diagnosis.

The study used a customized database from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) of South Korea containing data from 2010 to 2021, which was accessed for research on July 11, 2022. The data are available from the National Health Insurance Sharing Service of South Korea, but individual-level data cannot be publicly released due to regulatory restrictions.

Schizophrenia was defined using the ICD-10 code F2*, requiring one inpatient record or two outpatient records within one year, and patients diagnosed with schizophrenia in 2010 or under 18 years of age were excluded from the cohort. Patients with schizophrenia were matched to controls at a 1:2 ratio using propensity score matching based on the Charlson Comorbidity Index score, age, gender, and index year.

The propensity score matching used a caliper width of 0.2 standard deviations of the logit of the propensity score, with a standardized mean difference of 0.1 or greater indicating imbalance. The index year for patients without schizophrenia was randomly assigned between January 1, 2011, and the end date, which was defined as the date of Parkinson's disease diagnosis, death, or December 31, 2021.

The study utilized the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) dataset, which is accessible to researchers meeting specific criteria via the NHIS Data Sharing Service website (https://nhiss.nhis.or.kr). Access to the NHIS dataset is granted only for a predefined period approved for each research project, and re-access to the same dataset may not be available once this period expires.

The statistical analysis employed competing risk analysis and Cox regression to evaluate the relationship between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease (PD), accounting for antipsychotic medication exposure and comorbid conditions.
The analysis identified an adjusted hazard ratio of 3.198 for the risk of developing Parkinson's disease (PD) in individuals with schizophrenia compared to control subjects.
Among schizophrenia patients, risperidone use was associated with an increased risk of Parkinson's disease (PD), while quetiapine use was associated with a reduced risk of PD.
Significant comorbidities, specifically head injury and cerebrovascular disease, were identified as contributors to the increased risk of Parkinson's disease (PD).

The outcome of incident Parkinson's disease was defined as a new diagnosis using ICD-10 code G20 occurring at least one year after the initial schizophrenia diagnosis, requiring at least one inpatient diagnosis or two outpatient diagnoses with the G20 code within a one-year period to minimize diagnostic errors.

Covariates included demographic factors (sex, age, index year), clinical conditions (gastrointestinal diseases, osteoporosis, inflammatory arthritis, head injury, COPD, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, hypertensive disease, end-stage renal disease, coronary heart disease, cerebrovascular disease), Charlson Comorbidity Index, mental disorders (ICD-10 F00-F69), and related medications (ATC N05A-N06D), all based on records from one year prior to the outcome.

Statistical methods included t-tests for continuous variables, chi-squared tests for binary variables, phi correlation coefficient for binary associations, Cox regression for crude and adjusted hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals, Kaplan-Meier survival analysis with log-rank tests, and Fine-Gray's competing risk analysis treating death as a competing risk.

Sensitivity analysis was conducted using 1, 2, or 3 years before the end date to account for limited knowledge about the onset of Parkinson's disease in schizophrenia patients, and medication analysis used the intent-to-treat method based on prescriptions at the time of initial diagnosis.
Variables with a phi coefficient of 0.4 or higher were excluded from the multivariable analysis, specifically CCI score, medication N05A-N06D, mood (affective) disorders, and hyperlipidemia.

The exclusion rule for high collinearity between two diseases removed the disease with more associations with other variables, and the exclusion rule for collinearity between a disease and a medication removed the medication.

The competing risk analysis reported a 3.198-fold increased risk of Parkinson's disease for schizophrenia (95% CI = 3.126-3.217) and a higher risk for males than females (aHR = 1.103; CI = 1.082-1.126).
Sensitivity analysis was conducted with 1, 2, or 3 years before the end date due to limited knowledge about the onset of Parkinson's disease in schizophrenia patients.

All statistical analyses were performed using SAS Enterprise Guide version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA), with a two-sided confidence interval of 0.05 considered to indicate statistical significance.

The study utilized de-identified secondary data provided by the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS), and all analyses were conducted within the NHIS-controlled secure research environment with restricted access.
Access to the National Health Insurance Service data was available only through the designated NHIS analysis center, and remote access from personal computers or external networks was not permitted.
A total of 42,522 patients with schizophrenia were matched to 85,041 controls by age, gender, matching-period Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) score, and index year.

The study cohort consisted of 85,041 control participants and 42,522 patients with schizophrenia, with baseline characteristics including mean age of 66.36 years (SD 18.27) for controls and 66.26 years (SD 18.48) for schizophrenia patients, and a mean index year of 2016.2 for both groups.

The multivariate analysis identified the use of antipsychotic drugs (ATC code N05A) as significantly associated with Parkinson's disease development, with a hazard ratio of 1.076 (95% CI: 1.023-1.132, p=0.0045).

Among comorbidities, neurotic, stress-related, and somatoform disorders showed the highest association with Parkinson's disease development, with a hazard ratio of 1.380 (95% CI: 1.333-1.429, p<0.001).
Sensitivity analysis included competing risk analysis and demonstrated that the adjusted hazard ratio for Parkinson's disease remained significant across 1-, 2-, and 3-year periods of comorbidities.

The Kaplan-Meier plot of Parkinson's disease-free survival rates revealed a significantly steeper decline for patients with schizophrenia than for controls over the 10-year follow-up period, with a log-rank test p-value of <0.0001.

The baseline Charlson Comorbidity Index distribution differed between groups, with 23.56% of controls and 27.17% of schizophrenia patients having an index of 0, 31.28% of controls and 29.81% of schizophrenia patients having an index of 1-2, and 45.16% of controls and 43.02% of schizophrenia patients having an index of 3 or greater.
The prevalence of antipsychotic medication (ATC code N05A) use at baseline was 19.56% in the control group and 71.12% in the schizophrenia patient group.

Table 4 reports adjusted hazard ratios for Parkinson's Disease in antipsychotic drug prescription patients, including specific values for variables such as Age (0.983), Antipsychotic drugs (1.076), and Sex (1.046).
Table 5 presents adjusted hazard ratios for Parkinson's Disease in quetiapine and risperidone prescription patients, listing specific hazard ratios for Quetiapine (0.946) and Risperidone (1.203).
The study used Cox proportional regression and Fine-Gray competing risk analysis to calculate crude and adjusted hazard ratios for Parkinson's disease.
Quetiapine was the most commonly prescribed antipsychotic with 20,485 patients, followed by risperidone with 9,521 patients and aripiprazole with 5,052 patients.
Risperidone use was associated with an increased risk of Parkinson's disease with a hazard ratio of 1.203 and a 95% confidence interval of 1.184-1.337.
The adjusted hazard ratio for schizophrenia in the competing risk analysis was 3.198 with a 95% confidence interval of 3.126-3.217.
The adjusted hazard ratio for male sex in the competing risk analysis was 1.103 with a 95% confidence interval of 1.082-1.126.
The adjusted hazard ratio for age in the competing risk analysis was 0.986 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.986-0.987.
The adjusted hazard ratio for neurotic, stress-related and somatoform disorders in the competing risk analysis was 1.521 with a 95% confidence interval of 1.489-1.554.
The adjusted hazard ratio for head injury in the competing risk analysis was 1.228 with a 95% confidence interval of 1.168-1.290.
The adjusted hazard ratio for cerebrovascular disease in the competing risk analysis was 1.346 with a 95% confidence interval of 1.314-1.379.
The crude hazard ratio for N05A antipsychotics was 2.744 with a 95% confidence interval of 2.692-2.798.

The study utilized a large retrospective cohort from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) database in South Korea to investigate the association between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease (PD).
Variables with a Phi correlation coefficient greater than 0.4 were excluded from the adjusted hazard ratio (HR) analysis.
The sensitivity analysis for Parkinson's disease risk by exposure duration employed both a no competing risk model and a Fine-Gray competing risk model.
For a 1-year exposure duration, the adjusted hazard ratio (HR) was 3.310 (95% CI: 3.238-3.384) in the no competing risk model and 3.198 (95% CI: 3.126-3.217) in the Fine-Gray competing model.
Quetiapine use was associated with a reduced risk of Parkinson's disease (HR: 0.946, 95% CI: 0.899-0.995, p=0.0317) compared to non-users.
Aripiprazole use was significantly associated with an increased risk of Parkinson's disease (HR: 1.160, 95% CI: 1.103-1.221, p<0.001) compared to non-users.
Mental and behavioral disorders due to psychoactive substance use were associated with an increased risk of Parkinson's disease (HR: 1.305, 95% CI: 1.218-1.398, p<0.001).
Neurotic, stress-related, and somatoform disorders were associated with an increased risk of Parkinson's disease (HR: 1.338, 95% CI: 1.286-1.393, p<0.001).
The study utilized a cohort design with competing risk adjustment and included a wide range of covariates to adjust for comorbidities and medication use.
The study performed a focused comparison of two antipsychotic medications to explore their differential impacts on Parkinson's disease risk.
The study evaluated the association of schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease using large claims data including the majority of the Korean population.

The study could not fully account for time-varying treatment patterns, such as medication switching or the use of anticholinergics, which may lead to misclassifying persistent medication-induced symptoms as incident Parkinson's disease.

Collinearity analysis was conducted to reduce confounding effects by excluding highly correlated variables, but residual bias may persist due to the close association between schizophrenia diagnosis and antipsychotic medication use.
Quetiapine has a higher affinity for serotonin 5-HT2 receptors than for dopamine D1 and D2 receptors.
Risperidone exhibits a higher dopamine receptor occupancy rate than quetiapine, exerting a stronger influence on dopaminergic pathways.
Aripiprazole is a high-affinity D2 partial agonist, and molecular imaging studies indicate that D2/3 receptor occupancy can be very high at clinically effective doses.

The study defined Parkinson's disease as new diagnoses made at least one year after the initial schizophrenia diagnosis to minimize the misclassification of transient, drug-related parkinsonian symptoms as idiopathic Parkinson's disease.

The study's retrospective observational design and reliance on administrative claims data prevent causal inference and restrict access to granular clinical information such as disease severity, symptom onset timing, and neuroimaging results like DaTscan. The absence of laboratory test results and a multicenter design further limits the generalizability of the findings.

Diagnostic accuracy was defined by requiring at least one inpatient record or two outpatient records within a year to mitigate misclassification based on administrative codes. The study was limited by the inability to reflect individual daily dosing ranges or the exact cumulative duration of exposure within the large-scale administrative database framework.

Individual analyses for all medications were not performed because the analysis focused on drugs with larger sample sizes, and multiple comparisons across different antipsychotic agents were not explicitly adjusted for Type I error. Medication adherence could not be directly assessed, so an intent-to-treat approach was applied to mitigate this limitation.

Replication of the diagnostic performance requires the exact sample size (n) per group to calculate the 95% confidence interval for the reported AUC of 0.760, as the current data lacks the statistical power verification needed to distinguish the signal from noise.

A critical gap for reproduction is the absence of documentation regarding whether multiple comparisons were corrected for the various covariates, which is necessary to determine the validity of the AUC of 0.760 and the sensitivity of 0.606.

The claim that the anti-gravity system maintains near-physiological gait kinematics cannot be verified because the data only shows improvement under unloading, lacking the specific biomechanical parameters required to confirm a restoration of natural mechanics versus altered biomechanics.

The administrative barrier to accessing the raw data is a primary obstacle to replication, as the specific dataset needed to verify the gait speed and balance improvements in Parkinson's patients is currently unavailable.

The anti-gravity treadmill study failed to specify if therapist instructions or cueing strategies were standardized across the two conditions, and the same two physiotherapists supervised both groups, which creates an uncontrolled confound that blocks replication of the treadmill's isolated effect.

The rehabilitation study lacks a reported 95% confidence interval for the gait speed effect size and relies on small cohorts, which prevents independent verification of the statistical significance of the unloading treadmill intervention.

The validation study reports an AUC of 0.75-0.77 but omits the 95% confidence interval, which blocks any verification of the diagnostic precision or reproducibility of the eye test's performance metrics.

The reported ICC(2,1) > 0.90 for test-retest reliability is conditional on unspecified environmental controls and lacks the exact n per group and 95% confidence intervals, making it impossible to replicate the reliability metric or determine if the agreement is a statistical artifact of a small denominator.

All three studies systematically omit 95% confidence intervals for primary effect sizes, which is a fundamental gap that blocks any assessment of estimate precision and prevents distinguishing true population-level phenomena from inflated artifacts of small sample sizes and uncorrected multiple comparisons.

The microtremor validation study used the hand-held iTremor ONE device with a 70-150Hz signal filtering range, but the omission of webcam distance, software versions, and calibration logs prevents verification of whether the frequency range was adjusted for ambient light conditions, blocking replication of the acquisition parameters.

The high test-retest reliability claim for the iTremor ONE device is unverifiable due to missing raw data, specific software versions for the 70-150Hz signal processing, and calibration logs required to confirm results outside the controlled 12-hour washout protocol.

Reproduction of the primary ANOVA and unadjusted ICC(2,1) calculations is blocked by the absence of the exact sample size (n) per group and the lack of reported 95% confidence intervals, which prevents independent verification of the precision of the reliability estimates.

Validating the digital biomarkers for Parkinson’s gait, ocular microtremor, and schizophrenia requires a larger, adequately powered randomized controlled trial that standardizes environmental controls and reports full precision metrics. Current replication is blocked by methodological gaps, including uncontrolled variables in the ocular microtremor work and retrospective-only associations in the schizophrenia study that preclude causal inference.
